utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. The accused Nikolic is still not with us. The situation I take it is the same, we still have his go-ahead. Mr. Ostojic is back, Mr. Bourgon is still absent. When are we going to see Mr. Bourgon back, Madam Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I expect him in the course of this day. I expect he will join us today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Is he preparing a big motion? Mr. Ostojic is back. The rest are all here. Mr. Thayer and Mr. McCloskey. The witness is -- I couldn't see him, yeah. Sorry, my apologies to you, Mr. Vanderpuye, the column is in the way. So good morning to you, Witness, welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I trust that within 15 minutes you will be out of this courtroom. So Mr. Thayer, he is all yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe we're continuing with cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ah yes, yes. It's Mr. Josse and Mr. Meek who are left, yes. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Witness, it's right that yesterday you told the Court you were familiar with the voice of, amongst others, General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-146 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown the packet of four intercepts that are being introduced through him. If the usher is uncertain, perhaps I could look at it briefly just to check that it's the right bundle of documents. That is the correct packet, it's, in fact, been updated, as it says. Witness, unfortunately the index is in English only. I don't think that's going to matter very much, but perhaps I could ask you, do you read English?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-146 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As I say, I think you'll still be able to use the index. You see those four intercepts that, as I've already said have been introduced into evidence or going to be introduced into evidence through you. It's right, isn't it, that General Gvero was not a participant in any of those four conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-146 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. How are you today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-146 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, I just want to clarify a few points. Is it true that I understood you correctly yesterday, and -- you began your duties at the site that we've been discussing at -- in late June of 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-146 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you had no formal training whatsoever in this field before you were assigned that job?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-146 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For this job, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And I'm correct also in understanding that when you began at the -- your job at the site which is in issue, you worked seven-day shifts, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-146 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And so you'd work seven days at the site, then you'd work seven -- or go home to Tuzla for seven days, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-146 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, you stated in your testimony and in your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor that you became familiar with certain channels and the voices of military personnel; isn't that what you said, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-146 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: But are you telling this Trial Chamber under oath that you became familiar with the voices of certain staff members from the General Staff of the VRS by the fall of Srebrenica in July, mid-July of 1995, when you'd only began working in late June, and you only worked seven days on and went to Tuzla for seven days off?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-146 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, how many times would it take for you to hear a voice before you recognised it? Once? Would one time be enough, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Meek, I hate to interrupt you, but that question was asked repeatedly by Madam Fauveau and actually at a point in time I even stopped her.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, she did ask that question, but I don't think we ever got an answer to it. In that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course he did. He even went as far as to -- to say that he didn't need months. I mean it's starting from days, but anyway, go ahead. Ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So, Witness, if you picked up a conversation and started recording it and listening to it the very first time you were then familiar with that voice and you would hear it and recognise who that person was without them saying their name from there on out. Is that what you're telling this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-146 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not immediately, but frequently the speakers would introduce themselves. Since they had to ask for a telephone connection through a switchboard, you would often hear sentences like, "Wait a minute, the General is not here," "the General will take it," and such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: During your -- during your time working at this location, were you ever involved or taught about misinformation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-146 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not my job to think about such things. My job was to do what I had to do and to forward it. And somebody at the other end was supposed to say whether that was propaganda or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I think we need -- I just have two more questions, Your Honour, and I think we need to go into private session for these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do that. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes, we can go into open session, obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, we are in open session now. Mr. Haynes, just a confirmation from you that you don't have any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there re-examination, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness, that's all. As I explained to you, your testimony has come to an end. You are free to go. Madam Usher will escort you out of the courtroom. On behalf of the Tribunal, I wish to thank you for having come over to give evidence in this trial. And I also on behalf of everyone wish you a safe --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- also wish you a safe journey back home. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that was my job then, my duty and responsibility to contribute in some way to the Defence of my country, and I am happy to appear here as a Prosecution witness against these accused who tried to destroy my country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe everybody has been furnished with a copy of our tender sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. Any objections on the part of the Defence teams? I hear none. So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. There is a concern shown by some -- one of my colleagues in relation to line 13 -- line 12 on the -- on page 6, where, after the witness's statement I said thank you. I wasn't thanking him for saying -- using the words "against the three accused who tried to destroy my country." We keep ourselves completely out of -- from that. I mean, I take it for granted that we are on the same wavelength on that. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just add that once again that everything in bold be placed under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, basically means everything. The first two of these documents, that's the witness statement and the pseudonym sheet are admitted, with the respective numbers 02380 and 02381, the rest being intercepts will be marked for identification and in the meantime preserved under -- kept under seal. All right. Next witness. For the record, this last witness who finished, in case it doesn't show up in the transcript was PW-146, and the next one will be PW-136.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir. And welcome to this Tribunal. You are soon going to start giving evidence. Our Rules require that before you do so you make a solemn declaration to the effect that you will be testifying the truth. The text of the solemn declaration is being handed to you now by Madam Usher. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable. There are a few things I need to explain to you before you start giving evidence. Prosecution requested and was granted by the Trial Chamber three protective measures in your respect. First is the use of a pseudonym instead of your real name and surname. The other two are facial and voice distortion. I suppose these have been explained to you by our officers. I just want to confirm with you that they are to your satisfaction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye, who you've met already, will be examining you in chief, specifically referring to a witness statement that you made way back on the 6th of May of 1999. He will follow with a few questions and then I'll pass you over to the Defence teams for their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning. Good morning Your Honours, good morning, counsel, good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Just one piece of advice, word of advice. The witness's voice is such that it is extremely important that everyone keeps the microphone switched off when he is speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: For the record, may I have PO2384, please, shown to the witness. Good morning, Witness, could you please look at that document and without telling us what's on it, could you confirm whether or not you are the person that is named on it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes, my name is on this piece of paper. My full name.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and that will remain under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to put to you a few questions. I would ask if you could to allow a short pause between the question and the answer so that the interpreter can keep up with you. And also try to keep your voice up so that we can all hear you clearly. Do you recall having given a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor signed and acknowledged on 6 May of 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was the statement that you gave at that time truthful?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes, it was truthful.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to read your statement before having come to testify here today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you read the statement in your native language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was the -- was that the language that you originally gave the statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And for the record, what language is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, having read the statement, were there some clarifications that you felt needed to be made?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did that refer -- did that refer to specific information contained in the statement, and I will -- I will ...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was that specific information with respect to your job concerning the surveillance of enemy telegrams?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And would it be more accurate to say that that work involved actually intercepting coded telegrams?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was the specific information with respect to your knowledge of the operation of the State Security Services and the 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And would it be more accurate to say that you knew that they were involved in work similar to yours but not their specific protocol of operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: I assumed that the operatives of the 2nd Corps were doing the same job as we did, whereas I had no idea what the state security people were doing. I had my assumptions, but I don't really know what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Subject to those clarifications, was the statement that you -- does the statement that you gave 6th May of 1999 accurately reflect what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And does it fairly and accurately reflect what you would say, were you to be examined here today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With that, Your Honours, I would offer the statement into evidence. PO2383, pursuant to 92 ter. I do have a brief summary of the statement, if I may read that into the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: For the first couple of paragraphs I would like to proceed in private session, if we could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do that. Let's go into private session straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Upon his assignment to the northern site, the witness received 15 days' of training and began processing intercepted communications, following a process of scanning, listening, recording, and transcribing conversations on to sheets of paper and then into notebooks. These sheets of paper were discarded once the witness completed transcribing notebook entries, usually at the end of a shift. The notebooks themselves, however, would never -- would be turned over to the unit commander, typed and sent via computer to the command. The witness believed that filled notebooks were retained by the commander and taken to the command. The focus of the unit was mostly on the communications of high level VRS officers, typically covering areas for which the 2nd Corps was responsible. This would be intensified in areas where there was an offensive going on. Upon shift changes, operators were given information regarding the frequencies to be monitored and about important occurrences that needed to be focused upon. Over time, the witness became familiar with the voices of certain officers and would use their names or code-names in transcription if he knew their identity, where the identity of the collocutors was not known, X and Y were used. Tapes were reused due to supply shortages and in some instances conversations were not taped, but directly transcribed or summarised. The witness served as an operator at the northern site until November of 1995. That concludes my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have really only a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, have you had an opportunity to review the packet of intercept communications, three of them, that are contained in a packet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In particular, did you review the handwritten material that was contained in that packet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you recognise your handwriting in all three of the communications that are contained in the packet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you transcribe that material into a notebook, pursuant to your responsibilities and duties as an intercept operator?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review the original material or the original notebook, I'm sorry, containing these handwritten intercepts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And are you satisfied that the copies of the intercepts that are contained in the packet conform to the originals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: At this time I would like to have the original notebook placed on the ELMO, if I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: For the record that's PO2369, ERN 0080-4625 through 4742. In e-court is it possible to have displayed, please, 65 ter 1179A? I just wanted to position the notebook on the ELMO to the specific point of reference, if I could. Thank you very much, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Right at the top could you just tell us if you can see on your notebook a conversation that was taken down at 9.55?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Could I just move down the page a little bit? Okay. That's very good. Thank you. Okay. Do you see the phrase in your notebook referring to a person by the name or -- by the name of Burtula. It says, "Burtula didn't carry out the boss's order." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, a few lines below that there is a reference to three men, and in between there is a series of dots. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court whether the dots -- or what the dots are intended to mean, whether or not that particular portion is unintelligible or whether or not that particular portion simply could not be heard, that is that there was interference or something of that nature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: This part of the conversation, because of interference, could not be heard. It wasn't audible. So I didn't note that down in the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Probably there was some interference.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you -- could would he just go down to the bottom of this -- what's in e-court, the bottom of the translation? And turn the page, please, on the ELMO. I'm sorry, I mean the second page of the translation. Thank you. Thank you. At the end of this intercept there is an indication, and you tell us if you find it in your notebook, that the rest was not recorded. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you explain to the Court the circumstances under which that would have occurred or may have occurred in this case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: I assume that it's what would sometimes happen, that the tape had come to an end and that you could not record the rest of the conversation, because the tape had come to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were there any circumstances under which the tape was actually -- rather than coming to an end was turned off deliberately in relation to recording an intercept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: No, no. It was never done intentionally. The recording was never stopped intentionally. The only thing that could have happened was that the tape would come to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it was your -- was it your practice, I should say, to -- to make this specific designation that the rest was not recorded under those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes, yes. When this happened, then you would put in parentheses that the rest was not recorded, meant that the conversation went on after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could just refer the witness to page -- the page in the notebook with the ERN ending 4638. Witness, there is a date that appears to be indicated on this particular page. It reads 15.07.1995. Is that the date that the intercept that we have been speaking about was recorded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Could we just turn over the page to 04639, please. And I want to refer you to an intercept that begins at 8.55 a.m. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Was that -- was that particular intercept also recorded on the 15th July 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: For the record that's PO2385. And -- I'm sorry. And may I just switch notebooks for a moment? Okay. For the record, the witness is being shown the second notebook, P02386, ERN range 0078-1141 through 1328. Specifically page 0078-1235 is now on the ELMO. Witness, there is also a date written on this page, 13.07.1995. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can I just turn the page, please? In the middle of the page there is a -- appears to be an intercept that beginning recording -- well, top of the page now, at 1602. Do you see that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you confirm that the date that this intercept -- well, first -- well, can you confirm that the date of this intercept -- that the date that was recorded was 13th July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With that, Your Honours, I have no -- oh, okay. That's 65 ter 1142, and with that I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. And also for having kept within the time limits indicated by the Trial Chamber. Now, have you organised yourselves, Defence teams? Mr. Zivanovic is going first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that at this facility which we will call the northern facility, that you worked in shifts there, that switched from between seven to 10 days. Can you please tell me how many people there were in one shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: From six to nine people, usually.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And can you remember the period of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: I cannot remember specifically, but I know that there were between six to nine people there who worked at one time. And we worked 24 hours a day. We covered 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me, you know that there was another unit right next to you, you've already told us that. Can you tell whether there were -- that unit was bigger than your section or smaller?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: I really couldn't be sure, but I think that the unit was bigger.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned in your statement -- you mentioned the commander. You didn't mention his name though. So what I would like to ask you is if you remember his name, but please do not speak it out, even though if you -- even though if you remember it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I remember his nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we move to private session for a moment, Your Honours, so that we could have the witness tell us this nickname?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I was going to suggest in any case. So let's go into private session for a short while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that the commander entered the data into the computer. Is that the first one whose nickname you mentioned or the other one that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: It was the first one I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that the notebooks that you had where you wrote down the intercepts, that the commander would enter the date of each day and he would also enter the date at the end of the day. Which commander did that, the first one or the second one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: I really don't know who put in the date at the end of the day of those two, I really couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You gave a statement to the Tribunal investigators, and you've already told us about that. In that statement I saw that 10 days before you gave the statement you got in touch with a person, perhaps we could move into private session just for a moment so that I can mention the name of the person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Let's move into private session again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said then that that person, 10 days before you gave your statement, showed you some notebooks. I would like to ask you where this took place.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: We met in a cafe on the first floor in the place where I live.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And that's where he showed you the notebooks, at the cafe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was anybody else present other than the two of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Well, I really cannot remember that. I don't remember if anybody from the Tribunal was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, good morning. If I may have the little stand there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I would like to initially ask you questions about the process that you undertook to, after listening to a purported conversation to record it on a piece of paper. And a process is written in your statement, as you describe it, dated the 6th of May, 1999. It appears on the page with ERN number 00778108, the first full paragraph. And sir you state as follows: "I did not keep any notes or write anything down except in the notebooks and the only other information was what was on the computer or on the disks. When a call came in, I did write down the time the call came, and normally the initials of the people involved on a sheet or scratch of paper. I would also write down the whole conversation on the piece of paper after listening to the tape, and then write it out neatly in the notebook. After the shift, the paper would be thrown out. I normally wrote out the conversation from the paper into the notebook at the end of the shift." It appears again, as I state, on your statement on page 00778108. Do you remember giving that statement to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. I would transcribe the conversations not on a piece of paper, but into a notebook. I had to write quickly. Then what I took down first I would recopy into another notebook, because then I would have enough time and my handwriting would be much nicer and it would be more -- much easier to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, also in your statement on page 00778109 you reference a Colonel Ljubo, but you don't give a last name. Can you tell us in May of 1999, did you know the last name of the colonel who you reference as Colonel Ljubo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: I knew it at the time, but that's how I wrote it down. I knew it was Ljubomir Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And how do you know, sir, that his first name is Ljubomir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: I knew it because when I got up there in 1995 you knew everything, the call signs of each general, it was on a piece of paper. You knew who used each -- who used which code, and their full first and last name was known.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In preparing for your testimony here, sir, and in giving your statement in 1999, did you look through your book to notice how many times you actually captured a conversation which involved Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: What was shown to me, I looked at, I looked at the notebooks where I noted down the conversations, and I could see that it was my handwriting and my signature. So I could look at what was presented to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, other than that one entry at 9.55, were there any other entries that you reviewed or saw, sir, in your logbook that was either shown to you or you independently made a review of your logbook, which would indicate you captured a conversation with Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: I saw an intercept where he introduced himself. That's the one that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, now, let's look at your intercept that you, with your handwritten note at 9.55 you mentioned just now that you signed it. I looked at the intercept and I couldn't find your signature on that intercept, sir. Can you please, with the Court's assistance -- or Court's approval and the usher's assistance point out to me where on this intercept at 9.55 that you actually place your signature? And maybe the original logbook, it might go quicker if we could have the usher place it on the ELMO. It has ERN number 0080-4642 and 43 respectively. Sir, do you have the intercept in front of you that we are referencing at 9.55? I think the page prior, if we may. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That intercept starts with the frequency of 255850/955. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then it carries on to the next page where you say that you were unable to capture the remainder of the conversation and then you explained that to the Court a little bit. Do you see that on the next page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Then underneath that there is a line with an arrow pointing upwards, I guess, in the northerly direction; do you see that as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Where within those two sections does your name or signature appear, sir, from this conversation of 9.55, as you so claim you signed it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: I am not claiming. I said that I signed it, I don't see it here though, so it's possible that I forgot, that I failed to put it there. It would sometimes happen, but still I know that it is my handwriting and that it was I who transcribed the conversation from the tape. Perhaps I just forgot to put my signature there. Mostly I signed each intercept and perhaps, as in this case, sometimes it would happen that I forgot to put the signature there. But this is my handwriting and it means that I transcribed the conversation from the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. The entry immediately below what you claim to be your handwriting in this intercept, can you tell us what time that conversation was captured, sir, by looking at that entry immediately below it on 00804643?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, sir, does that indicate that's approximately, what, 3.21, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And is it your testimony, sir, that this was the very next entry that was captured and from 9.55 until 3.21 there were no conversations that were captured or recorded because there were no conversations taking place during that eight or so hours, correct? Or six or so hours.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Maybe there were some conversations, but they were probably not very important. I can't tell now. Maybe we were changing the tape or waiting for another tape to arrive, I don't know exactly why such a long break was made. Maybe the tape had run out, maybe something was broken in our equipment. I cannot tell you the exact reason for that long pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement you state that you recognised the voice of Colonel Ljubo, and you further state, "I knew his voice well," and that's on page 00778109 in the second full paragraph. Can you tell us, sir, how is it that you knew his voice well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: We had enough experience to identify some of the higher officers by voice, and I know that because when I get a call from friends of mine I never make a mistake, whoever they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... answer. But my question is really related to someone who you never met, correct? Did you ever meet Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you speak to him on the telephone at any time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And from looking at your logbook, sir, and given that the Prosecutor never showed you any other entries that you purportedly have captured a conversation from Mr. Beara, how often, as you sit here, sir, do you think that you had heard or overheard a conversation where Mr. Beara was a participant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Well, I cannot be sure. It was a long time ago, but I heard the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I found none other than this one claim, sir. But given that can you describe for this Court any distinctive features in Mr. Beara's voice that you claim in your statement given under oath that the Prosecutor seeks to introduce into evidence that you knew his voice well? Share with us, sir, what aspects of his voice you knew well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Well, if you asked me about that in July 1995, I would be able to write it down. But after 12 years I cannot really tell you the features of that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I didn't get the last part, sir. I think you said it's impossible, "nemoguce," correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Now, after 12 years, it's impossible for me to remember the features, because I know that some of the generals used the certain words that are typical for Serbia proper, they had distinctive features of speech, accents, et cetera. But now, after 12 years, I cannot tell you what were the distinctive features of each one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What about in 1999, sir, when you gave the statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, did they at any time, sir, ask you how is it that you knew Colonel Ljubo's voice well and seek from you what characteristics or features of his voice you claim that you knew well? Did they ask you those questions in 1999, May 6th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. How about this, sir: Did you volunteer any of that specific information to point out what the distinctive features or characteristics of Mr. Beara's voice was as you claim it to be in 1995 to the Prosecutor on May of 1999 when you gave the statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then a final issue, if I may, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, if the southern site captured the same conversation, you would expect that the conversations would be identical, would you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Not necessarily. If it was a duplex connection, maybe the person on the southern location was listening to one participant, I was listening to the other participant, to the other speaker. We were listening to the same conversation but we would have different transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let's look at your conversation at -- to the right on the ELMO at 9.55. Did you hear one side of the conversation or both sides, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: From this we see that we heard two speakers, two participants. And there could have been more than two. I heard two.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well -- thank you. And so let's assume then that the southern site also heard two participants in this conversation. Given that you're both listening to the same conversation, would you expect line for line the conversation that was being captured to be identical?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: If they were listening to the same participants as I, then yes, that would have been logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the reason for that is, sir, that your job, as well as the job of members in the southern site was not to interpret or to add things to the conversation, but merely to record simultaneous and contemporaneous conversations that you may have heard, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Right. From this conversation that I transcribed from the tape, you see that there are some distinctive words, and I took it verbatim down from the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, highlight those for me, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, I don't know if your colleague has informed you about the decision of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: They have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So you've got three minutes left. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My learned friend is welcome to have our time if he needs it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Josse, but there are others as well who might be very happy to take your time too. So I don't want to put you in competition. So try to finish in three minutes' time, then when we have gone the round, if there are problems we'll -- we'll address them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think we're waiting for an answer. Sir, can you point out for us those distinctive words which you took verbatim from the tape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: All the words you see in this conversation were taken down verbatim from the tape, and if necessary I can read out the whole intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We have it, thank you. I thought that you had mentioned there were some distinctive words, and we'll look at that again just to make sure, because -- given the time constraints. Sir, can you look quickly on the participant's section of this conversation; on 9.55, the name "Ljubo" is written on top. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When was that change or -- if you could see there seems to be some writing over the original writing of the name. When was that done and by whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: I just made this B a little thicker, boldened it. Maybe my pencil broke and then I drew the line again. I did that myself. Nothing here was tampered with or corrected. You see the B and the letter that is pronounced "lj" written like L-j are also bold.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And when did you make this bold B and J in the name Ljubo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Right there and then when I was transcribing the conversation. I boldened these letters because my pencil may have sort of skipped.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, given the Court's ruling, we have no other questions at this time of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would like to hear what the -- just a second. Distinctive? I don't remember the words. If the witness would be able to identify some distinctive words as it -- as he put them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the words in this conversation, from "P," the first letter of Pukovnik, colonel; "Alo," meaning hello; it goes on, "Come on, answer it, colonel." Then you see a part of the conversation that I was unable to hear. You see three dots, probably somebody was trying to interfere. The colonel says, "Ljubo, Beara" so he introduced himself. K, Krstic, he also introduced himself. P, colonel, says, "hello" again. Krstic says, "I'm listening to you, Beara." Krstic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Witness. Why do you say they are distinctive? In what sense or for what reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am reading to you the entire conversation as I intercepted it. All these words were taken verbatim from the tape. As they were talking each word was recorded in the notebook. There is not a single word that I recorded descriptively or paraphrased. I took it all down verbatim. There are even some illogical things, like towards the bottom he ordered to him that three men, three dots, from the army and it seems to be a -- in the spirit of a local dialect, but I took it down as it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I have a couple of questions regarding your testimony today. On page 10, lines 12 to 18 you described the other unit that was there, and your knowledge about their work on the northern location. That is the two operators from the State Security Service, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: At the northern location, according to your statement of the 6th of May, 1999, you spent almost a full six months?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Beginning with March, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Your centre consisted of one room housing your team and next to you were those two employees of the State Security Service who were doing their own job?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it very well. At the entrance of the building the first one on the left was their office, and the next one on the left was our office.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And after six months there, seeing them every day, you had an opinion about them, and you stated that opinion in that statement of the 6th of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Your memory was fresher then and you said that your opinion was that their task was to monitor your soldiers and what they were doing, to check on your intercepts, and to verify whether radio stations were used properly on the ground?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I thought, that's what I assumed, and there is an old saying that says that assumptions were the mother of all mistakes. However, that was my opinion then, otherwise I had no particular insight into their work, nor did I have any contacts with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So at that time in 1999 when you were interviewed by OTP investigators it was your opinion that that job was to monitor your work, your units and your soldiers, to keep them under surveillance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes, I said that's what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait, wait. Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time I stated that it was my opinion as to what their job was. I assumed that's what they were doing, and as I said, assumptions were the mother of all mistakes. Which means that it was only my opinion. I had no other knowledge of what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I have a couple of questions concerning the method of your work. Just from looking at these notes that we received immediately before you appeared in court. I want to know about the situation where you are listening to a conversation and you can't identify the speakers. You ask others for assistance in recording that conversation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: I asked for assistance if I'm unable to distinguish a word. We rewind and rewind several times and I invite other people, including the commander, because maybe I am the only one who cannot hear it properly, so I invite others to listen to the same recording and see if they can make out what was being said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did it ever occur to you that when other people were lending you a hand in such a way you were also told by others who the participants in the conversation were, according to their speech mannerisms, accents, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Well, I had other colleagues and my commander who were able to identify speakers, but I don't remember asking them specifically for that kind of assistance. I -- I was recording for instance a conversation where the speakers were X and Y, and I can't remember whether I would invite somebody to help me identify the speakers, to put a name on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If situations like that occurred, would you note it down in any way that somebody else helped you identify the speakers? Would you make that note in parentheses or put a question mark or something like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question at all, because I cannot remember that I received such assistance or that I asked for it, I really can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If a participant in a conversation did not introduce himself and you did recognise the voice, and wrote his name down in the intercept, did you spell that out in any way that you recognised the voice rather than heard the name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: No. No, I did not do that. And anyway there were very few conversations in which I would write the names down because I recognised them. Only when I was 100 per cent sure. If I had the slightest question in my mind I did not proceed in that way. It was only when I was 100 per cent sure about the identity of certain persons that I wrote down their names. Otherwise I would write X and Y, whenever I did not have a 100 per cent certainty as to their identity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The way I hear you now, such situations did not occur; you never wrote a name down and then put a question mark next to it. You either wrote a name down when you were 100 per cent sure or alternatively, you wrote X and Y?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: You are correct. I never put question marks next to a name because that would denote a dilemma and that would not have been proper. There was no room for dilemmas and assumptions in our job. We were doing that for the purposes and requirements of our army. We could not afford to do such things; we had to know exactly who was doing what and how.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you this because I made this up, I'm saying this because we had heard the testimony of many other operators who used that particular method of work. I'm just asking you about the unit where you come from, because we heard operators from various agencies. So did the unit that you belonged to follow that rule that you describe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: I'm speaking only in my own name. I personally did not put question marks to denote uncertainty. And I cannot speak about other units and their way of work, because I had no insight into their organisation and their methods. I can only speak about myself in my own name. I did not use that practice of question marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did it ever occur that when you were unable to hear something you used not only dots but also asterisks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Possibly dots and asterisks. Maybe even a dotted line. All these were used to denote a part of a conversation that we were unable to hear well because of temporary interference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What I mean to ask you is this: In your unit did you have any instructions as to designating a particular situation with dots as opposed to other situations that are denoted with asterisks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: No. It was left to us to decide how we would denote passages that we were unable to hear. We used dots, dotted lines, asterisks. When you see something like that, it meant that parts of the conversation were either not recorded at all or certain passages were impossible to make out due to interference and even after rewinding the tape several times the operator could not distinguish the words.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, maybe we are talking rather fast and it all has to be recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your microphone. I don't want this to become an inconvenience. Witness, it's mostly your fault because you are jumping straight into answering a question before it has even been finished. And that means that the microphone of counsel's microphone has not yet been switched off. Your voice carries. We are trying to protect your identity. So you have to exercise a little -- I can't keep on watching whether it's switched off in time or not. Please try to allow a pause between question and answer and don't start answering the question until you have seen the microphones -- red microphone light switch switched off. Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We will do our best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not your fault, Mr. Stojanovic. It's the witness's fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think a part of your answer is really recorded. What was the practice of your unit regarding identification of speakers in a conversation? Did you ever use the practice of putting question marks next to the name of a person that you think you identified, that you potentially identified?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: I can speak only in my own name. I did not use the practice of denoting my own dilemmas as to the identity of the speaker. I did not use that method of putting a question mark next to a name. You also asked me about dots, asterisks, and dotted lines. It was not important which one of these you used, all of those were used to denote part of intercepts that could not be transcribed either because participants could not be heard because of interference or certain words could not be distinguished.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And let me conclude. What was the focus of your work and scanning of conversations in that half of 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: If you mean specifically Srebrenica, the focus was on the entire offensive of the units of the VRS and that entire area of Srebrenica. We were monitoring the area of Gradacac and everything that was under the 2nd 21 Corps, and I don't know whether our colleagues at(redacted) monitored the 3rd Corps or other areas, but we were monitoring the area of Srebrenica during the offensive, the area of Gradacac, Brcko, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a short while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Stojanovic. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I will complete the examination very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you recall, sir, we finished or we stopped with the question of what you were listening to in mid-July. So my question, and I will end the cross-examination with it, is: How was the actual procedure, who told you what you would be doing, which frequencies you would be listening to, or was it just your sense of the need at that particular moment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: The superior commander, the unit commander or the platoon commander would -- before we began work at the workstation, would tell us which events were important, which frequencies should be monitored, also when we came to work we would consult with the operator who worked before to find out if he noted down any important conversations, what we should be paying attention to, which frequency was important, and then we would sit at the workstation and begin our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you were told to start monitoring the eastern Bosnian area, the Srebrenica region?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Well, I really couldn't say. The antennas were already directed in that direction at the beginning of those events, so I, as an operator, had to work strictly to monitor and record and transcribe the intercepts into the notebooks. As for the other things, this was in the hands of our superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And to finish with this question, was just your unit a unit that had its own antenna system, or did each of the units at the northern location have its own antenna system?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: The 21st Division that I worked for had its own antenna system. Each set of equipment had its own antenna. The operators who worked for the 2nd Corps had their own antennas and they monitored certain area or sector which was probably different from the sector that we were monitoring.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't have any further questions but I think perhaps your intervention is necessary. On page 38, line 20, in view of the fact that the unit was mentioned that this witness belonged to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can -- we can -- we can proceed. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit P2369, this is the notebook 24. Would it be possible to show the witness the original notebook?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, just before we begin, could you tell us if the conversations were -- the intercepts were written down in a chronological order in this notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: No. As for the time of the intercepts, it was not done in a chronological order because I copied conversations from paper on to the notebook, so sometimes it was 9.20, and then 10.00, it wasn't like that. Sometimes the times would not be consequential. So in any case, when the conversation was transcribed, the time was always put in. So if you are thinking of when each conversation occurred, then the time of the conversation was always entered.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 13, this is the page that bears the number 00804638. Regarding the date that is transcribed on this page of the 15th of July, 1995, were you the one who put this date on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: No, I did not enter the date, I can tell because this word, Subota, Saturday, this is not my handwriting. This is not what my handwriting looks like. I did not put the date in.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... saw this notebook again, can you tell us if, since you looked at that notebook again when you came here, could you tell us if there is a date that was transcribed or written down by yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: I would have to look at it to be able to see. Can I look at it? I've looked at the notebook, and I did not put the date in anywhere.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel needs to wait until the English translation is finished.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 21, it's P2386 and the number ERN is 00781141?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, my attention has been drawn by the interpreters that you need to wait until the English translation has finished before you put your next question. In fact, we missed your question or part of your question, which you are kindly asked to repeat, if possible. Thank you. At least for the record, because the witness apparently has understood what you said.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Mr. President, thank you. I will repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown notebook number 21, the ERN number is 00781141, and I need page number 111. It's page number 00781251. It's the page that ends with 1251, and in the e-court system we're talking about P2386, page 111, one eleven. Could the witness be shown the intercept that's at the bottom of the page? Or at the top of the page, under the line, rather. Above the line at the top of the page, that is the portion that we are interested in. Is this a conversation that you transcribed yourself, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: A part of the intercept, yes. The part at the top where it states, "Sladjan Mladic was killed at Ilidza in the morning. Cube, son of Slobodanka." There's nothing else that is urgent. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know if line 11 should be redacted. Page 41, line 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm just locating it on the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just four lines up.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would ask if it's -- I would ask if it could be redacted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's safer to redact it. So let's redact lines 9 and 10, please. Or 9 and 10 in one, 10 and 11 in another. I mean it's -- the pagination and line do not tally, lines do not tally. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Witness, at the very top of the page, if you look at this intercept, you can see the frequency, the channel, and the participants, right? Is it exact to say that the time of the conversation or the intercept is not written down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes, the time is not noted down. I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it exact to say that you were supposed to put down the time normally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes, but I assume that this part of the conversation follows the previous conversation, and it is in my handwriting, but the signature is different. I don't know why it's underlined here, so it probably came immediately after the conversation recorded at 2008 hours, so that's why I did not put down the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we say that this is a mistake, that the fact that you have omitted to put the time down, that this is a mistake on your part?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-136
utterances.text: Yes, that is my own mistake. I should have put the time in, even though it followed the previous conversation, the time should have been put in, 2110 or 11, so it's probably my mistake that I did not note down the time, that I omitted it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could we go into the private session for -- could we go into private session for a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've read the situation perfectly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't either, and if anybody wants to take any of my time, I'm open to offers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, do you need some more minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't think so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye, do you have a re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, I don't have any re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't have any questions for you either, which means that your testimony comes to an end here. Madam Usher now will help you-- escort you and help you with the arrangements for your return back home. On behalf of the Tribunal I wish to thank you for having come over to give evidence, and I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we come to the documents. You have the list. The witness statement will go under seal. It's being admitted. 02383. I see -- first of all, let me see if there are any objections. None. The pseudonym sheet, the same. That will become 02384, Prosecution. Then there are three intercepts which will be marked for identification and kept under seal. And finally the handwritten intercept notebook, PO2386, which will be marked for identification. You have not indicated that you require it under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I was going to ask if the procedure has been to the extent that the notebook itself may contain items that require sealing, if the notebook itself has been -- has been tendered for identification under seal. If that's been the practice, then that is what I would like to do in this particular case, but if not, then I suppose we can proceed that way as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Always assume that I don't put unnecessary questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that will be kept under seal as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next witness. This was Witness PW-136.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is Witness number 173, correct, Ms. Soljan? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: PW-148, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I welcome you to this Tribunal. You are soon going to start giving evidence. Before you do so our rules require that you make a solemn declaration that you will testify the truth. Madam Usher is handing you the text. Please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please take a seat, make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me explain to you briefly. We have granted upon request from the Prosecution some protective measures in your record. The first is the use of a pseudonym, which means an alias instead of your name and surname, and we have also put in place facial and voice distortion. I take it these have been explained to you and that they are to your satisfaction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's been explained to me, and I am satisfied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now Ms. Soljan, whom you know, will go first. She will be asking you some questions and also reading out a summary of your witness statement of the 21st of January of this year. She will then be followed by cross-examination by the Defence teams. One very important thing that I would like to draw your attention to. We are trying our best to hide your identity, and we need your cooperation there. You are asked questions, you will be asked questions both by the Prosecution and by the Defence. When someone else is speaking to you or talking to you, you will see that there is a red light lit on his or her microphone. Please don't start talking while that light -- red light is still on. Wait until it is switched off and then you can safely speak. Otherwise your voice, especially if it carries, will be captured. Did I make myself clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Soljan, you go first.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Good morning, witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-148
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: If I could please have the usher's assistance in providing the witness with what has been marked for identification as P02388. Now, Witness, if you could please take a look at this piece of paper and just tell us whether your name is on it without saying that name out loud.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-148
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, do you recall providing information to the Office of the Prosecutor on Sunday, the 21st of January, this year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-148
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And was the statement you gave at that time truthful?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-148
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Have you also had an opportunity to read through the statement before having come to testify here today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-148
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And are you satisfied that the statement that you read is true, correct and accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-148
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, I will go ahead and read a short summary of that statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you don't mind just the first sentence, I would like to read it in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means. Let's go back to private session for a short while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: I wanted to say that for the record PO2387 and, I only have very few questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Sir, did you have an opportunity to review two handwritten copies of intercepts in a tabbed blue binder this morning and yesterday with me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-148
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And did you identify both of those intercepts as your original handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-148
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Sir, did you also have the opportunity to review those same intercepts in the original notebook they were taken in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-148
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And did you confirm that they were in your own handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-148
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: So, sir, my final question for you is, can you confirm, as you sit before the Trial Chamber today, that you have listened to, recorded and transcribed these two intercepts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-148
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: I have no more questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Ms. Soljan. Defence, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-148
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement given to the OTP you said, among other things, that the unit where you served numbered 10 to 12 men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-148
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also said you had worked in two shifts. Does that mean that that unit of 10 to 12 soldiers, as you remember, was divided into two parts and worked in shifts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-148
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to that, you had daily shifts as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-148
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how many operators worked at the same time in daily shifts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-148
utterances.text: Two operators.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how many sets of equipment did you have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-148
utterances.text: Two sets.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe and give us more detail about the set of equipment you worked with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-148
utterances.text: That set had two or three frequencies that were stored in memory. We just scanned those frequencies at random and looked for something interesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the statement you gave to the Prosecution a couple of days ago you said that you could not remember very well, but it seems to you that you were using a set of equipment that scanned only one frequency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-148
utterances.text: I'm telling you approximately, I'm -- I emphasised I did not remember for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that intercepts were recorded on one tape; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-148
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that there was only one tape recorder?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-148
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what would happen to an intercept after it was recorded and transcribed by you in a copy book?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-148
utterances.text: I am not -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question. You also said that you had to write down the date, the time, and frequency at the beginning of every intercept, as well as the names of speakers if you knew them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-148
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember who gave you orders to proceed in that way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-148
utterances.text: The people, the senior soldiers with whom I worked taught me to do it that way. It was the practice I just learned from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, they told you to use those elements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-148
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Meek or Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. For the record, Mr. Bourgon is now in the courtroom. Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have no questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Stojanovic.
